newsitem.title: UK: UK RETAIL DATA AWAITED TO CONFIRM CBI SURVEY.
newsitem.headline: UK RETAIL DATA AWAITED TO CONFIRM CBI SURVEY.

text.p: A Confederation of British Industry survey on Thursday pointing to a slowdown in growth in UK retail sales in July could be confirmed by official data due later this month, but analysts were cautious about following the CBI results too closely.
The CBI distributive trades survey showed 56 percent of retailers reported increased sales volumes in July, while 21 percent said they were down.
This left a positive balance of 35 percent reporting increased volumes compared with 39 percent in June.
"The fact that the annual sales figure fell to a positive balance of 35 would actually be consistent with a very weak sales figure during the month," said David Philpotts, economist at Schroders.

"It is consistent with the M0 (money supply) figure earlier in the week, which pointed to a slowdown after a strong June. But we tend not to read too much into this survey and would rather wait until the official data is out before making policy conclusions on the back of it."
The official data for July are due on August 20.
The weaker-than-expected CBI survey covers around 15,000 outlets of firms responsible for 40 percent of employment in retailing, wholesaling and motor trades.
But it has a mixed track record in matching official data, and analysts are aware it measures retailers' subjective views on their business.

"The CBI survey has not always been a good steer for official figures and I don't place too much faith in it, although the overall picture of a slight fall we have here is what we expect from retail sales," said John O'Sullivan, UK economist at NatWest Markets.

"It's not a fully objective measure as it relies on retailers' views. There is a certain subjectivity about survey data that you don't get in official data and of course it covers a smaller number of retailers."
But this month, the survey could be right in signalling a modest slowdown in growth.

"With the growth of notes and coins in circulation also slowing in July, it does appear that high street activity weakened after the windfall-induced surge in spending in the previous month," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

A stronger-than-expected rise in June retail sales of 5.4 percent year-on-year and 0.6 percent month-on-month was mirrored by a leap in the volume of sales component of the distributive trades survey from a positive balance of 21 to 39, suggesting stronger sales.

Some analysts attributed the jump in June's figures to one-off purchases after a 17 billion pound ($27.2 billion) windfall payout from the conversion of the mutually-owned Halifax building society into a bank, and said the weaker figures expected for July should help quell fears of soaring inflation.
The Bank of England announced the fourth quarter-point rise in interest rates in as many months on Thursday, pushing rates up to 7.0 percent.
